\section{Asymptotic symmetries}

The asymptotic symmetry group is the quotient of all gauge symmetries by those that are "trivial" (sometimes also called "proper") \cite{REGGE1974286}. Here by trivial gauge symmetries we mean those symmetries which leave all physical states and observables invariant.^[Sometimes gauge symmetries are referred to as trivial if the constraint vanishes on-shell \cite{Henneaux:2010vx}. Trivial gauge symmetries here also include those generated by constraints that don't.] In gravity, the main gauge symmetries are diffeomorphisms. The asymptotic symmetry group can be non-trivial on manifolds with boundary \cite{REGGE1974286,Banados:2016zi}. In this case, the generators of gauge transformations may contain boundary terms leading to non-trivial transformation properties of physical observables \cite{Iyer:1994ys}. Such diffeomorphisms give rise to [covariant surface charges](/1st-level-topics/2nd-level-topics/Covariant_surface_charges.qmd) \cite{REGGE1974286,Iyer:1994ys,Arnowitt:1962hi,Barnich:2001jy} which act non-trivially on physical states.

Usually, the asymptotic symmetry group has both a global and a local component. The global component is generated by Killing vector fields, i.e. [rigid isometries of the background spacetime](/1st-level-topics/2nd-level-topics/Global_spacetime_symmetries_and_isometries.qmd) \cite{Wald:1984rg}. Examples of global spacetime symmetries are the Poincaré, Anti-de-Sitter and de-Sitter symmetries of maximally symmetric spacetimes of respectively vanishing, negative and positive cosmological constant in any number of dimensions.

In general, solutions to the Einstein equations may only admit isometries in the neighborhood of a point or hypersurface such as a boundary, horizon or initial data surface. Depending on the choice of boundary conditions, the asymptotic symmetry group may be enhanced, in the sense that local diffeomorphisms are also promoted to non-trivial symmetries. Examples are 2 and 3-dimensional [asymptotically AdS and dS spacetimes](/1st-level-topics/2nd-level-topics/Asymptotic_symmetries_in_AdS_and_dS.qmd) \cite{BrownHenneaux1986,Maldacena:2016upp,Cotler:2019nbi}, and [asymptotically flat spacetimes](/1st-level-topics/2nd-level-topics/BMS_algebra.qmd) \cite{Bondi:1962px,Sachs:1962zza}. In the former cases, the asymptotic symmetry algebra contains the Virasoro algebra, while in the latter case, it contains (at least) an angle-dependent enhancement of the Poincaré translation generators known as the [BMS algebra](/1st-level-topics/2nd-level-topics/BMS_algebra.qmd). The same algebras sometimes generate the global symmetries of quantum field theories \cite{Zamolodchikov:1989hfa}. That asymptotic/gauge symmetries of a gravitational theory are dual to global symmetries of a conformal field theory in a lower number of dimensions is one of the fundamental properties of [holographic dualities](/1st-level-topics/2nd-level-topics/Holography.qmd) \cite{Aharony:1999ti}.

\section{Global symmetries}

It is believed that quantum gravity admits [no global symmetries](/1st-level-topics/2nd-level-topics/No_global_symmetries_in_quantum_gravity.qmd) \cite{vanBeest:2021lhn}. Here a global symmetry is defined by a group $G$ admitting a representation on the quantum gravity Hilbert space that preserves the space of local operators and which commutes with the Hamiltonian. It is further assumed that there exists at least one local operator transforming non-trivially (i.e. that is charged) under the action of $G$. The global component of a gauge group such as the group of spacetime diffeomorphisms does not qualify as a global symmetry in the above sense since there exist no local, gauge invariant operators charged under it.

One can use properties of black holes to heuristically argue against the existence of global symmetries in quantum gravity. For instance, assume global symmetries were allowed and one could create black holes of arbitrary global charge. On the one hand, the no-hair theorem implies that one cannot measure their charge, and hence such black holes would have infinite entropy in contradiction with the Bekenstein-Hawking formula \cite{Bekenstein:1973ur,Hawking:1975sw}. On the other hand, allowing for the black hole to evaporate, and assuming all radiation is neutral under the global symmetry \cite{Hawking:1975sw}, one is left with long-lived remnants, carrying arbitrary charges. Such an infinite tower of remnants would give rise to an infinite density of states at low energies and would lead to severe consistency problems, such as loss of predictivity in scattering processes or destabilization of the vacuum \cite{Preskill:1992tc,Banks:2010zn}.

Sharper statements can be formulated in a holographic \cite{Harlow:2018tng} or [string theory](/1st-level-topics/2nd-level-topics/Symmetries_in_string_theory.qmd) \cite{Banks:2010zn} context. In [AdS/CFT](/1st-level-topics/2nd-level-topics/Global_symmetries_in_holography.qmd) the definition of a global symmetry can be refined to trade the elusive notion of the bulk quantum gravity Hilbert space by the Hilbert space of the dual conformal field theory (CFT) -- see def. 4.2 of \cite{Harlow:2018tng}. As a result, bulk global symmetries also act as boundary global symmetries and one can arrange for the bulk charged operators under these symmetries to lead to an inconsistency with entanglement wedge reconstruction \cite{Dong:2016eik}. Further arguments along these lines can be found in Section 4 of \cite{Harlow:2018tng}.

In perturbative string theory, global symmetries on the string worldsheet give rise to gauge symmetries in the target space. The simplest example is bosonic string theory, where conformal invariance of the worldsheet is generated by Noether charges constructed from currents of definite weights and lead to vertex operators that create massless gauge vectors in target space \cite{Polchinski:1998rq}.

One can refine the arguments to also rule out higher-form symmetries and discrete symmetries, but not [approximate global symmetries](/1st-level-topics/2nd-level-topics/Generalized_and_approximate_global_symmetries.qmd) in an effective field theory of gravity \cite{Banks:2010zn,Gaiotto:2014kfa}.
